question: Can a continuous-space quantum state be optimized directly through its logarithmic spatial gradient, using Langevin sampling and a diffusion-inspired weighted score-matching loss instead of an explicitly evaluated neural wavefunction?

key_findings.claim: For a real nonzero wavefunction away from nodes, the local energy can indeed be written using only its logarithmic-amplitude score and score divergence.
key_findings.evidence: With s(x)=grad_x log|psi(x)|, the kinetic term satisfies E_L(x)=-1/2[div s(x)+||s(x)|| squared]+V(x). This exact identity motivates direct score prediction and removes one differentiation through an explicit scalar wavefunction during local-energy evaluation.

key_findings.claim: DiffVMC alternates approximate score-only Langevin sampling with a stop-gradient, local-energy-weighted implicit score-matching update.
key_findings.evidence: Samples move as x'=x+sqrt(alpha) epsilon+alpha s_theta(x). An endpoint-gradient approximation eliminates explicit psi ratios from Metropolis-Hastings. The WSM objective reweights the implicit score-matching integrand by softmax(-beta(E_L-mean E_L)), treating weights as constants during differentiation, and repeats sampling after each parameter update.

key_findings.claim: The loss is heuristically motivated but has no demonstrated ground-state convergence or variational guarantee.
key_findings.evidence: The authors explicitly say the short-imaginary-time approximation is used at beta near one where it need not hold and that there is no rigorous convergence proof. The zero-variance argument only shows that an eigenstate has constant local energy; this applies to excited eigenstates as well as the ground state. Saying the ground state is a local minimum therefore does not establish selection of the lowest state. Normalized finite-batch softmax weights are also a ratio estimator, so equality of weights at the solution does not prove WSM is an unbiased energy-gradient estimator away from it.

key_findings.claim: An unconstrained vector network need not be the score of any wavefunction, undermining the density, energy, and variational interpretations.
key_findings.evidence: A valid s=grad log|psi| must be curl-free within each nodal cell and integrate to a normalizable amplitude. The permutation-equivariant bosonic network and the added FFN term in grad FermiNet+FFN impose neither integrability nor boundary normalization beyond a heuristic -x term. Langevin dynamics can have a stationary distribution for a nonconservative drift, but that distribution generally does not have the claimed score and Equation 5 then need not equal H psi / psi for any psi.

key_findings.claim: The score-only method succeeds on analytic harmonic traps, but the realistic fermionic evidence still depends on an explicit FermiNet wavefunction and is less accurate and slower than VMC.
key_findings.evidence: Bosonic and fermionic 2D oscillator curves reach analytic energies. For B, C, N, and O atoms, the score is computed as grad_x of FermiNet, sometimes plus an FFN; B, C, and O enter the stated 1.594 mEh chemical-accuracy window under at least one setting, while N remains about 7 mEh high. Every displayed conventional FermiNet energy is lower. Appendix D states DiffVMC is slower because it backpropagates through the gradient network, and the atom optimization uses FermiNet-oriented KFAC that requires the explicit wavefunction.

key_findings.claim: Fermionic sign and nodal structure are the central unresolved obstacle, not a minor implementation detail.
key_findings.evidence: The score of |psi| loses relative sign/phase across nodal cells and diverges at nodes. A hand-coded 1/(x_i-x_j) singular term solves the special 1D oscillator, where the exact form is known, but in 2D predicts energies 4,9,16,25,36 instead of 3,5,8,11,14. The authors conclude that pure score functions fail beyond two particles in their higher-dimensional attempts and use determinant gradients for reported atoms.

key_findings.claim: The proposed rejection rule is an approximate bias-control device, not Metropolis-adjusted Langevin with exact detailed balance.
key_findings.evidence: It replaces the log-amplitude difference by a trapezoidal endpoint-gradient approximation and reduces the acceptance ratio to exp(alpha/2(||s(x)|| squared-||s(x')|| squared)). The approximation can be accurate for small steps and smooth conservative scores, but cannot correct a nonintegrable score or finite-step quadrature error exactly. On nitrogen, it stabilizes mean energy close to conventional MCMC for three step sizes, whereas omitting rejection produces extreme mean-energy outliers despite stable medians.

anchors.section: B Langevin dynamics sampling and Table 2

method.core_idea: Replace an explicit scalar neural-wavefunction ansatz with a permutation-equivariant vector field intended to equal grad log|psi|, evaluate local energy from its divergence and norm, sample with Langevin dynamics, and update it with local-energy-weighted score matching.
method.mechanism: Initialize walkers and a score network; take repeated unadjusted Langevin proposals with an approximate endpoint-score acceptance rule; compute local energies from div s, ||s|| squared, and V; stop-gradient through centered softmax energy weights; minimize their weighted implicit score-matching integrand; and iterate. For fermions, seed the field with the input gradient of a determinant-based FermiNet and optionally add an equivariant residual score network.
assumptions: The Hamiltonian and target state can be treated as real, so phase information is unnecessary.
The learned vector field is or remains close to a conservative, normalizable logarithmic-amplitude gradient.
Samples track the distribution implied by the changing score after finitely many Langevin steps.
The trapezoidal log-amplitude approximation makes the rejection rule sufficiently close to detailed balance.
A short-imaginary-time expansion remains directionally useful at the chosen beta and optimizer step size.
Stop-gradient weighted score matching preferentially selects the ground state rather than another eigenstate or spurious fixed point.
Determinant-derived nodes can be retained or improved while optimizing a score field.
Local-energy averages from the field retain the meaning and upper-bound property of a Rayleigh quotient.

techniques.role: Represents local amplitude geometry by grad log|psi| rather than psi values.
Computes kinetic energy from score divergence and squared norm.
Generates walkers from score drift plus Gaussian diffusion.
Approximates the missing amplitude ratio with endpoint score integration.
Upweights low-local-energy samples in an implicit score-matching objective.
Imports determinant antisymmetry and nodes through the input gradient of an explicit FermiNet.
Adds a shared-particle set-network vector field to the determinant-derived score.

limitations: No theorem shows WSM converges to the ground state, decreases Rayleigh energy, or preserves a variational upper bound.
Arbitrary score networks are not constrained to be curl-free or integrable to a normalizable wavefunction.
Scores of absolute amplitude omit complex phase and do not alone encode relative signs across disconnected nodal cells.
The only atomic experiments derive scores from an explicit determinant wavefunction, so the headline score-only fermionic method is not realized.
Pure-score fermion modeling fails in the provided 2D multi-particle tests.
Atomic energies are uniformly worse than the conventional FermiNet results in the table, with nitrogen outside chemical accuracy.
The approximate rejection rule does not satisfy exact detailed balance and is tested for sampling only on one small atom.
DiffVMC is reported slower than VMC and retains the expensive divergence/second-derivative bottleneck.
No molecules, bonds, solids, scaling curve, wall-clock comparison, observable beyond energy/density, or multiple initialization study is reported.
Beta, clipping, step size, pretrained determinant structure, and optimizer adaptation affect stability without systematic ablation.
failure_modes: A nonconservative learned drift circulates probability and cannot be interpreted as grad log|psi|.
Walkers approaching fermion nodes experience singular scores and heavy-tailed local energies.
Approximate acceptance accumulates time-step bias when the score changes rapidly between endpoints.
WSM can stabilize an excited eigenstate because every exact eigenstate has constant local energy.
Softmax energy weights can collapse onto rare spuriously low local-energy outliers, especially under nodal singularities.
Stop-gradient weighting can optimize a surrogate whose descent direction is not the derivative of physical energy.
A field can produce plausible oscillator energies while failing to encode global sign topology or general observables.
Clipping score norm near singularities biases both sampling and kinetic-energy estimation.
Reusing KFAC designed for scalar FermiNet outputs can poorly condition gradient-field optimization.
The apparent efficiency benefit disappears when score divergence and backpropagation through input gradients dominate runtime.
reusable_insights: Local energy exposes a useful force-field view: amplitude derivatives can be modeled and audited directly even when a scalar ansatz is retained for integrability.
Hybrid scalar-plus-score architectures can amortize input gradients while preserving exact antisymmetry, phase, and a valid Rayleigh quotient.
Any direct score ansatz should enforce integrability, for example by differentiating a scalar potential or penalizing curl, and test path-independent line integrals.
Sampling diagnostics must include energy medians, tail quantiles, node proximity, effective sample size, and time-step extrapolation, not only mean acceptance.
Ground-state optimization should compare surrogate-gradient alignment with the exact VMC energy gradient and test excited-state fixed points explicitly.
Report both accuracy and derivative-order wall-clock cost when replacing scalar values with vector fields.
Treat nodal topology as a first-class learned object for fermions rather than expecting permutation equivariance of density to recover it.
open_questions: Can a curl-free score parameterization retain the computational benefit without evaluating a full scalar neural wavefunction?
Is there a score-only objective whose gradient exactly equals or provably descends variational energy?
How can relative fermionic signs, nodal-cell topology, and complex phases be represented alongside amplitude scores?
Can exact score-based Metropolis correction be obtained through tractable path integration or an auxiliary normalizing potential?
Which excited states and nonphysical vector fields are stable fixed points of WSM?
Does a hybrid score control variate accelerate FermiNet/PauliNet at matched accuracy on molecules and solids?
How do Langevin bias, beta, clipping, walker count, and optimizer interact as electron count grows?
Can divergence estimation be reduced below the local-energy bottleneck without unacceptable variance?

competitive_landscape.title: Ab-initio Solution of the Many-electron Schrödinger Equation with Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: FermiNet represents an antisymmetric scalar wavefunction with determinant layers and optimizes its variational energy, retaining exact sampling ratios and nodal signs. DiffVMC seeks a more direct derivative representation but uses FermiNet gradients for every realistic fermion experiment and reports worse energies and speed.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep-neural-network Solution of the Electronic Schrödinger Equation
competitive_landscape.difference: PauliNet builds antisymmetry, multireference Hartree-Fock structure, cusps, Jastrow correlation, and backflow into an explicit ansatz and demonstrates molecules up to 30 electrons. DiffVMC uses less scalar structure in principle but has not matched its molecular scope or solved fermionic nodes without an explicit determinant model.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards the Ground State of Molecules via Diffusion Monte Carlo on Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Ren et al. keep an optimized FermiNet trial wavefunction and use fixed-node DMC projection to improve atomic and molecular ground-state estimates. DiffVMC instead updates the guiding score itself with WSM, avoiding walker branching but forfeiting DMC's projection logic and demonstrated accuracy.

competitive_landscape.title: Estimation of Non-Normalized Statistical Models by Score Matching
competitive_landscape.difference: Hyvarinen derives score matching as a consistent estimator for a fixed data distribution without evaluating its normalizer. DiffVMC makes the target distribution endogenous to the current quantum score and adds stop-gradient local-energy weights; consistency and convergence no longer follow from the original result.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards a Transferable Fermionic Neural Wavefunction for Molecules
competitive_landscape.difference: Scherbela et al. reduce per-system optimization cost through a scalar fermionic ansatz pretrained across compounds and geometries, while preserving a valid wavefunction. DiffVMC proposes representational efficiency but reports no transfer, molecular generalization, or runtime benefit.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: DiffVMC is a new score-only quantum Monte Carlo framework that samples by Langevin dynamics and optimizes a weighted score-matching objective toward many-body ground states without an explicit probability distribution.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The score form of local energy is exact, the proposed alternating algorithm is concrete, simple positive oscillator states converge, and approximate rejection controls heavy sampling tails when driven by a trained FermiNet score.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Directly optimizing spatial log-amplitude derivatives is a genuinely interesting synthesis of score matching, VMC, and DMC. The work is a feasibility study rather than a replacement for neural VMC: the loss is not variational or convergence-proven, unconstrained fields may not define wavefunctions, and all credible fermionic atom results still rely on the explicit FermiNet whose cost and topology the method sought to avoid.
